notes.text: The voice — Christ's voice, the word of grace revealed outwardly in the gospel, and inwardly by the Spirit of God. Leaping - He saith, leaping and skipping, to denote that Christ came readily, and swiftly, with great desire and pleasure and adds, upon the mountains and hills, to signify Christ's resolution to come in spite of all difficulties.

Like a roe — In swiftness. He is coming to me with all speed and will not tarry a moment beyond the proper season. He standeth behind - And while he doth for wise reasons forbear to come; he is not far from us. Both this and the following phrases may denote the obscure manner of Christ's manifesting himself to his people, under the law, in comparison of his discoveries in the gospel. The window - This phrase, and that through the lattess, intimate that the church does indeed see Christ, but, as through a glass, darkly, as it is said even of gospel-Revelations, 1 Cor. xiii, 12, which was much more true of legal administrations.

Spake — Invited me outwardly by his word, and inwardly by his Spirit. Rise up - Shake off sloth, and disentangle thyself more fully from all the snares of this world. Come - Unto me, and with me; follow me fully, serve me perfectly, labour for a nearer union, and more satisfying communion with me.

The winter — Spiritual troubles arising from a deep sense of the guilt of sin, the wrath of God, the curse of the law; all which made them afraid to come unto God. But, saith Christ, I have removed these impediments, God is reconciled; therefore cast off all discouragements, and excuses, and come to me.

The flowers — The communications of God's grace, the gifts, and graces, and comforts of the Holy Spirit, are vouchsafed unto, and appear in believers, as buds and blossoms do in the spring. The turtle - This seems particularly to be mentioned because it not only gives notice of the spring, but aptly represents the Spirit of God, which even the Chaldee paraphrast understands by this turtle, which appeared in the shape of a dove, and which worketh a dove-like meekness, and chastity, and faithfulness, in believers.
Her figs — Which it shoots forth in the spring.

glossa.text: *The voice of my beloved.* This is the voice which I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem that they should not awaken me: I rejoice hearing his consoling voice, though I do not yet see his face; yet, my mind being lifted up to heaven, I taste beforehand some sweetness of the blessedness to come, even in this present life. *Leaping upon the mountains.* He leaps upon the mountains, and as it were sets his feet there, by which sign he is known to have been there, because it imitates him through his passion and through the manner of his life. He made a leap from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the cross, from the cross into the sepulchre, from the sepulchre he returned into heaven. He it is who is lifted up above all mountains and hills, that is, above the heights of the saints, both the greater and the lesser. *Skipping over the hills.* On the *hills* the marks of his feet do not appear, but they received the shadow of him flying over: because although not as those greater ones, yet in some measure they imitate him and are visited by him, *Mountains* and *hills* are those who by a singular purity of mind pass beyond the common manner of life of the Church, as it were the flowering plain of the fields, and, withdrawing from the lowest things, contemplate the things above more nearly. In whom he *leaps,* because he illumines the hearts of the lofty with frequent visitation; and he abides not, but *leaps* and *skips over:* because this sweetness of contemplation is short and rare, because of the heaviness of the flesh, because the earthly habitation weighs down the mind that thinks upon many things.

*My beloved is like a roe.* Because he sees keenly, and dwells in the high places of the mountains, he leaps swiftly. Whence also he is more rarely seen by us: he ascends always from his nativity even to the bosom of the Father. *My beloved is like a roe.* And although by his divinity he so transcends all, yet he was made man, for me he was born of a Gentile and of the seed of the patriarchs. In the assumption of flesh and in his manhood he is compared to a *roe;* in the variety of virtues and of miracles to a *fawn.* The hart draws the serpent out of its caverns by the blowing of its nostrils, and, the destruction of the poison being overcome, delights in the food. Since in these little verses the loftiness of the contemplative life has been expressed, it remains to show the perfection of the active life, which is common to the whole Church. Whence follows. *Behold he standeth,* etc. *Behind the wall.* The wall which draws us away from the sight of him is the condition of mortality, which we deserved by sinning, we who were so created that, if we sinned not, all we the elect should behold the divine light unwearied: to the beholding of which very few of the more perfect now attain, with labour, purified by faith: but in this wall the mercy of God has made windows and lattices, whence he has made us to look forth, because to minds, although he weighed them down, he opened the grace of the knowledge of himself, and he looks upon us with the frequent light of his inspiration. Through the looking forth of which inspiration, because God does this chiefly, that he may call us from temporal things to the deserving of heavenly things, rightly is it subjoined: *Behold my beloved speaketh to me,* he who above admonished the daughters of Jerusalem to the guarding of my rest: he sends me to the tilling of the vineyards, showing me the opportunity. *Behind the wall.* Morally, if thou hast made thy building, God will come *behind the wall* of thine, *looking forth through the windows,* that is, through the five senses he carefully beholds; for where the Bridegroom looks not forth, death goes up: whence Jeremias: *Behold death is gone up through our windows ((Jer. IX))*; *through the nets.* All things are full of the nets of the devil, in which thou wouldst be taken, but that the Bridegroom subjected himself to the nets of the world, who eminently, and rending them asunder, might make a way, that thou mayest say: *Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers ((Psal. CXXIII))*. *Through the windows.* As the sun entering through the windows lights up the house, so Christ has enlightened us by the example and the admonition of the apostles. As through the *lattices,* that is, through small openings a small light enters, so an obscure knowledge through the prophets.

*Arise, make haste.* That is, break off contemplation, and labour for the winning of others; or, arise from the love of earthly things. Arise, all things have their time; he who but now was adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to disquiet his beloved: behold, he invites her to labour. *Arise, make haste.* ((GREG.)) When the soul is now led forth out of the body of corruption, for it the shower has passed, because the torpor of the present life has departed, and it is led forth to contemplate God in his substance, nor are the drops of words now needful, that the rain of preaching should be poured in. For what it was able to hear less, it shall see more fully. For then *the flowers appear in the earth,* when the soul has begun to taste beforehand certain first beginnings of sweetness out of the eternal life of blessedness, which things, going forth, she now smells in the flowers, and which, after she shall have gone forth, she shall have more abundantly in the fruit. *The time of cutting away is come.* Our cutting away then takes place when we forsake the unfruitful and hurtful corruption of the flesh, that we may be able to come to the fruit of the soul, which fruit is to us most abundant. For in the cutting away the barren branches are cut back, that those which are strong may bear fruit more abundantly. Therefore *arise,* because I, suffering for thee, have stilled the waves.

*Come.* To bestow also the care of salvation upon thy neighbours through the zeal of diligent preaching, that with a great company thou mayest deserve to be received unto the marriage. As if: thou believest that thou wilt come if thou art free for contemplation: but thou shalt come better through labour of this kind. It behoves thee to preach, because, since knowledge is now in thee, there is also in those to whom I send thee an opportunity of receiving.

*The rain is over.* I, rising from the dead, the tempest being checked, gave back tranquillity. Now it is easier to preach, since certain men are already converted, than before, when as yet no one had believed.

*The flowers. As if:* These, who now believe and now work good things, thou canst give as an example to others: these thou canst set before others for an example, who now suffer the pruning-hook that cuts back their vices. For thy own quiet thou oughtest not to let go preaching, because Christ, who was in great quiet with the Father, in a manner interrupted his quiet for preaching. *The time of pruning.* The useless branches of vain religion being now cut away, the hearts of men are prepared for the fruit of faith to come, now also the vices are cut away, because the time of the remission of sins is come. *The voice of the turtle is heard.* The Holy Spirit, when he speaks of the more hidden mysteries, and of things which many do not receive, is signified by the name of the turtle. Whence also he appears to Moses, and to him alone: when he treats of humble things which reach even to all, he is taken up under a dove, whence also at the Jordan, while many stood by, he appeared not in a turtle, but in a dove. *The voice of the turtle,* the voice of the apostles, or of any preachers whatsoever, who by their song announce the departure of winter and the coming of spring, who instead of a song render a lowly moan, who are lovers of chastity, who abide always upon the ridges of the mountains, or upon the tops of trees, and flee the company of men, while, set in the world in body, they have their conversation in the heavens, mindful of their sojourning and of the country promised to them.

*The fig tree.* He calls green figs the first and unripe figs, which are not fit for eating, which also, if they be shaken, fall at a light touch: therefore, when the turtle sounds, that is, when the apostles preach, the Synagogue put forth her green figs, that is, she cast away the unripe understanding of the legal observance. Or thus: the Synagogue brought forth the apostles, who should minister sweet food to those who believed them. And because, when the Synagogue put forth the apostles, the faith and the salvation of the whole world followed, rightly is it subjoined. *The vineyards in flower.* By the flowering, the beginnings of the manifold Churches, from that which was first planted at Jerusalem, from whose flower the juice pressed out makes a kind of drink suited to health and to delight, which gladdens the heart of man.

notes.text: Enditing — Hebrew. boileth, or bubbleth up like water over the fire. This denotes that the workings of his heart, were fervent and vehement, kindled by God's grace, and the inspiration of the Holy Ghost. Made - Have composed. Pen - He was only the pen or instrument in uttering this song; it was the spirit of God, by whose hand this pen was guided.

Fairer — Than all other men: which is most true of Christ; but not of Solomon; whom many have excelled, in holiness and righteousness, which is the chief part of the beauty celebrated in this psalm. Grace - God hath plentifully poured into thy mind and tongue the gift of speaking wisely, eloquently, and acceptably. Therefore - And because God hath so eminently qualified thee for rule, therefore he hath blessed thee with an everlasting kingdom.

O God — It is evident, that the speech is still continued to the same person whom he calls king, ver. 1, 11, and here God, to assure us that he doth not speak of Solomon, but a far greater king, who is not only a man, but the mighty God, Isaiah ix, 6. A right scepter - Thou rulest with exact righteousness and equity.

Therefore — Therefore God hath exalted thee far above all men and angels, to a state of joy and endless glory at his right hand; which is fitly compared by the oil of gladness. Thy God - According to thy human nature, John xx, 17, though in respect of thy Divine nature, thou art his fellow, Zech xiii, 7, and his equal, Phil ii, 6, and one with him, John x, 30. Oil - So called, because it was a token of gladness, and used in feasts, and other solemn occasions of rejoicing. Fellows - Above all them who partake with thee in this unction: above all that ever were anointed for priests or prophets, or kings.

Myrrh — Wherewith they used to perfume their garments: this may denote those glorious and sweet smelling virtues, which, as they were treasured up in Christ's heart, so did they manifest themselves outwardly, and give forth a grateful smell, in the whole course of his life and actions. Palaces - The king is here supposed to reside in his ivory palaces, and his garments are so fragrant, that they not only perfume the whole palace in which he is; but the sweet favour is perceived by those that pass by them, all which is poetically said, and with allusion to Solomon's glorious garments and palaces. The heavenly mansions, may not unfitly be called ivory palaces, as elsewhere in the same figurative manner they are said to be adorned with gold and precious stones, from which mansions Christ came into the world, into which Christ went, and where he settled his abode after he went out of the world, and from whence he poured forth all the fragrant gifts and graces of his spirit, although there is no necessity to strain every particular circumstance in such poetical descriptions; for some expressions may be used, only as ornaments, as they are in parables; and it may suffice to know, that the excellencies of the king Christ are described by things which earthly potentates place their glory. Whereby - By the sweet smell of thy garments out of those ivory palaces, or the effusion of the gifts and graces of thy spirit from heaven; which as it is a great blessing to those who receive them, so doth it rejoice the heart of Christ, both as it is a demonstration of his own power and glory, and as it is the instrument of bringing souls to God. Made thee - Thou art made glad.

Among — Among them that attend upon thy spouse, as the manner was in nuptial solemnities. As the queen is the church in general, and so these honourable women are particular believers, who are daily added to the church, Acts ii, 47. And although the church is made up of particular believers, yet she is distinguished from them, for the decency of the parable. And these believers may be said to be Kings daughters, because among others, many persons of royal race embraced the faith, and because they are in a spiritual sense, Kings unto God, Rev. i, 6. Right hand - The most honourable place. Ophir - Clothed in garments made of the choicest gold. By which he designs the graces wherewith the church is accomplished.

glossa.text:
*It hath uttered forth.* ((AUG., HIER.)) For the Prophet speaks within, etc., *as far as* before that is which he is about to do. But the counsel of the Father is the Word.

*Good.* By which all good things were made. *I speak.* That is, I bring forth the Word: the same here as before; but he says that in that very word are all the works of God; whence: *What was made in him was life,* so that nothing may be in the work which was not first in the counsel. Of this it is said: *God hath spoken once.*

*A pen.* He compares the Word not to sound, which passes away, but to writing, which remains. Or, *swiftly,* because not one thing after another, but all things together in one eternal Word.

*Swiftly.* The power of prophecy, which does not under human torment devise what it divulges to others out of the secret of the Godhead.

*Beautiful in form.* ((CASS.)) He begins the praise of the bridegroom first from his form. *He hath blessed.* The former things the Prophet said in the person of God, these from his own; or all from himself. Or, *he uttereth forth the word,* who says a hymn to God.

*I speak my works.* ((AUG.)) to the praise of him who is from him. *Tongue, a pen.* Because what I say, I also write. Or, *swiftly:* because the things which I write are quickly to come.

((CASS.)) *In the lips.* Because, when he spoke, the world received the grace of reconciliation.

*A throne. ((Ibid.))* Here from judgment: *A throne* pertains to judgment. *A rod. ((Ibid.))* The rule of divine equity, which is truly straight and is never bent: this governs the just, strikes the unjust. ((AUG.)) Let no one presume much to himself concerning mercy, or flatter himself: because the rod of direction, if it governs some, crushes others: it governs the spiritual, it crushes the carnal.

*Thou hast loved. ((Ibid.))* Or, because *thou hast loved justice,* etc., these rewards have been rendered, he made thee king, giving *the name which is above every name.*

*And thou hast hated.* If a man hates iniquity in himself, he acts with God: God hates iniquity, do thou also hate it.

*O God.* ((AUG.)) It is set twice openly in the Greek, the one a vocative, the other a nominative. This one is anointed, that one is the stone which Jacob anointed.

*Myrrh,* etc. ((CASS.)) Here the Prophet praises the bridegroom from his wife and from his adornment; first from the adornment. ((AUG.)) *Myrrh and stacte.* Perfumes are fitly applied to the bridal chamber, etc., *as far as* that is, redemption, through the water of baptism. *Of ivory.* ((HIER.)) In ivory, chastity, which, being dark before, is made bright by saws and files; so the saints, filed down by the cuttings and rubbings of divers punishments, are made bright by the variety of virtues. *The daughters of kings.* ((AUG.)) Of earthly ones, not caring for the honour of their fathers, etc., *as far as* and they took them for the raising up of seed.

*The queen stood,* etc. ((CASS.)) Here he commends the bridegroom from his wife. *With variety. ((Ibid.))* Although there be unity in charity, yet she is adorned with gold, that is, the doctrine of the Apostles, with the scarlet of the martyrs, with the gems of virgins, with the purple of the penitent.

notes.text: No evil, but every good gift — Whatever tends to holiness. And every perfect gift - Whatever tends to glory. Descendeth from the Father of lights - The appellation of Father is here used with peculiar propriety. It follows, "he begat us." He is the Father of all light, material or spiritual, in the kingdom of grace and of glory. With whom is no variableness - No change in his understanding. Or shadow of turning - in his will. He infallibly discerns all good and evil; and invariably loves one, and hates the other. There is, in both the Greek words, a metaphor taken from the stars, particularly proper where the Father of lights is mentioned. Both are applicable to any celestial body, which has a daily vicissitude of day and night, and sometimes longer days, sometimes longer nights. In God is nothing of this kind. He is mere light. If there Is any such vicissitude, it is in ourselves, not in him.

Of his own will — Most loving, most free, most pure, just opposite to our evil desire, ver. 15. Begat he us - Who believe. By the word of truth - The true word, emphatically so termed; the gospel. That we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creatures - Christians are the chief and most excellent of his visible creatures; and sanctify the rest. Yet he says, A kind of - For Christ alone is absolutely the first-fruits.

Let every man be swift to hear — This is treated of from ver. 21 to the end of the next chapter. Slow to speak - Which is treated of in the third chapter. Slow to wrath - Neither murmuring at God, nor angry at his neighbour. This is treated of in the third, and throughout the fourth and fifth chapters.
The righteousness of God here includes all duties prescribed by him, and pleasing to him.

Therefore laying aside — As a dirty garment. All the filthiness and superfluity of wickedness - For however specious or necessary it may appear to worldly wisdom, all wickedness is both vile, hateful, contemptible, and really superfluous. Every reasonable end may be effectually answered without any kind or degree of it. Lay this, every known sin, aside, or all your hearing is vain. With meekness - Constant evenness and serenity of mind. Receive - Into your ears, your heart, your life. The word - Of the gospel. Ingrafted - In believers, by regeneration, ver. 18 and by habit, Heb. v, 14. Which is able to save your souls - The hope of salvation nourishes meekness.
Beholding his face in a glass — How exactly does the scripture glass show a man the face of his soul!
He beheld himself, and went away — To other business. And forgot - But such forgetting does not excuse.

But he that looketh diligently — Not with a transient glance, but bending down, fixing his eyes, and searching all to the bottom. Into the perfect law - Of love as established by faith. St. James here guards us against misunderstanding what St. Paul says concerning the "yoke and bondage of the law." He who keeps the law of love is free, John viii, 31, &c. He that does not, is not free, but a slave to sin, and a criminal before God, ver. 10. And continueth therein - Not like him who forgot it, and went away. This man - There is a peculiar force in the repetition of the word. Shall be happy - Not barely in hearing, but doing the will of God.

If any one be ever so religious — Exact in the outward offices of religion. And bridleth not his tongue - From backbiting, talebearing, evilspeaking, he only deceiveth his own heart, if he fancies he has any true religion at all.

The only true religion in the sight of God, is this, to visit — With counsel, comfort, and relief. The fatherless and widows - Those who need it most. In their affliction - In their most helpless and hopeless state. And to keep himself unspotted from the world - From the maxims, tempers, and customs of it. But this cannot be done, till we have given our hearts to God, and love our neighbour as ourselves.

glossa.text:
*Every gift,* etc. ((BED.)) After he had taught that vices are not to us from God, but from ourselves, etc., *as far as* the perfect gift can be understood.

*Nor of alteration.* No shadow shuts off his light, so as to send in any evils. Always the goods of light are in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes such as supervening sins overshadow.

*Of his own will.* Every good is from God, and you have not come to this by your own merits, but by the sole grace of the divine will. *That we might be some beginning,* etc. By this begetting let us not think that we are that which he himself is, but a certain primacy among creatures he granted to us by adoption. Whence another translator: *That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.*

*Slow to anger.* Let no one be angry rashly and without cause, whether against sinning subjects, or against any brethren whatsoever, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the ripeness of wisdom is not perceived save with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justice, yet cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, into which disturbance does not fall.

*Wherefore casting away,* etc. He has admonished them to seek out doctrine, for the receiving of which, and that they may be able to advance in it, he now exhorts to cleanness of body and of soul. For he who declines not from evil cannot do good. *The engrafted word.* That which by preaching we lay upon your hearts, or the word which was engrafted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you; now receive it more perfectly, and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery.

*To him that considereth the countenance.* He who purposes in his mind to consider in the Scriptures, as in a glass, the countenance of his nativity, how man is born, how frail, or what he shall be, of how brief an age, set in how many miseries, has contracted great compunction and a will of repenting; but straightway, seduced by some temptation, he forgets his compunction, and returns to sins. To this inconstancy he compares him who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between him who of his own accord, without a teacher, has applied himself to the Scriptures, and him who from another hears the Scriptures, since neither has fulfilled them.

When a boy is born he wails, whereby is signified the grief of the soul, and that it enters into life unto the miseries of the flesh, which grief the soul afterwards forgets, being accustomed to the enticements of the flesh.

*Not bridling his tongue,* etc. ((AUG., Serm. 3 ad fratres in eremo.)) What else is wordiness? etc., *as far as* and do thou diligently attend: *He that bridleth not his tongue, his religion is vain,* etc.

*And to keep himself unspotted from this world.* By *saeculum* he understands the world, or all the things which are in the world, as are the concupiscence of the flesh, and of the eyes, and the pride of life.

notes.text: Coming from Jerusalem — Probably on purpose to find occasion against him. Matt. xv, 1.
Washing of cups and pots and brazen vessels and couches — The Greek word (baptisms) means indifferently either washing or sprinkling. The cups, pots, and vessels were washed; the couches sprinkled.
The tradition of the elders — The rule delivered down from your forefathers.
Isaiah xxix, 13.

There is nothing entering into a man from without which can defile him — Though it is very true, a man may bring guilt, which is moral defilement, upon himself by eating what hurts his health, or by excess either in meat or drink yet even here the pollution arises from the wickedness of the heart, and is just proportionable to it. And this is all that our Lord asserts.

Wickedness — The word means ill natured, cruelty, inhumanity, and all malevolent affections. Foolishness - Directly contrary to sobriety of thought and discourse: all kind of wild imaginations and extravagant passions.

glossa.text: *And they come together. ((ID.))* It is plain how true is that confession of the Lord to the Father in which it is said: *Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones ((Matth. XI))*. The unlearned come, they bring the sick, that they may touch even his hem, and therefore, having desired health, they suffer. But the Pharisees and the Scribes, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, run together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but to the battles of questionings.

*With common hands. ((HIERON.))* By unclean, or common, hands he signifies the communion of the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the communion of the apostles does not wholly stretch out its branches as far as the sea. *Not washed.* They find fault over the unwashed hands of the body, though in their works nothing of uncleanness is found. They themselves, washed outwardly with water, are inwardly polluted with the rancour of conscience.

*The Pharisees. ((BEDA.))* The superstitious tradition of men, to wash the oftener, for the sake of eating and the like. But the necessary teaching of truth bids those who desire to eat the bread of life which came down from heaven to cleanse their works by the frequent lament of alms and of the other fruits of justice.

*Washings.* In vain do they keep the washings of vessels, who neglect the filth of their own hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, and the chastisement of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.

*Why do thy disciples,* etc. Wondrous folly! They accuse the Son of God because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works not of the body but of the soul, are to be washed, that the Word of God may be wrought in them.

*Well did he prophesy. ((HIERON.))* The fork of reason represses the barking of the Pharisees, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and of Isaias, that we too may be able to overcome heretics by the words of Scripture.

*There is nothing outside,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Nor is it the meat offered to idols, in so far as it is food, in so far as it is a creature of God, but the invocation of demons, that makes this unclean. Whence: *You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons ((I Cor. X))*.

The Jews boast themselves the portion of God, and call those foods common which all men use, such as oysters, hares, and animals of this kind, which do not divide the hoof, nor chew the cud, nor, among fishes, are scaly.

*From the heart of men. ((BEDA.))* The chief seat of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. They are also reproved, etc., *as far as* so that, if he has often seen us gaze upon a beautiful woman, he understands that we love her.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years; and let them be for lights in the expanse of sky to give light on the earth”; and it was so. God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars. God set them in the expanse of sky to give light to the earth, and to rule over the day […]
echoes.note: God's 'Father of lights' designates him as Creator of the heavenly luminaries set in the firmament on the fourth day. James draws on the creation account to name God as source of the celestial lights, then contrasts their changing shadows with his own constancy.

echoes.text: “For I, Yahweh, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.
echoes.note: 'For I the Lord do not change.' James's claim that with the Father of lights there is 'no variation, nor turning shadow' affirms divine immutability in the very terms Malachi uses to assure Israel of God's unchanging fidelity.

echoes.text: The first of the first fruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
echoes.note: 'The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the Lord.' James's claim that we are 'a kind of first fruits of his creatures,' brought forth by the word of truth, applies the cultic firstfruits law to the new-birth of believers as God's consecrated portion.

echoes.text: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?
echoes.note: 'God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind.' Balaam's oracle on God's unchanging reliability undergirds James's contrast between God's constancy and the shifting shadows of the luminaries.

echoes.text: To him who made the great lights; for his loving kindness endures forever: The sun to rule by day; for his loving kindness endures forever; The moon and stars to rule by night; for his loving kindness endures forever:
echoes.note: The hymn praises God who made 'the great lights... the sun to rule over the day, the moon and stars to rule over the night.' James's 'Father of lights' draws on this liturgical confession of God as maker of the heavenly bodies.

echoes.text: It shall be, when you have come in to the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, possess it, and dwell in it, that you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you shall bring in from your land that Yahweh your God gives you. You shall put it in a basket, and shall go to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there. You shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and […]
echoes.note: The firstfruits offering ritual, with its confession of God's saving acts, lies behind James's designation of believers as firstfruits. The dedication of the first and best to God interprets the believers' status among his creatures.

echoes.text: Israel was holiness to Yahweh, the first fruits of his increase. All who devour him shall be held guilty. Evil shall come on them,”’ says Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest.' James's 'firstfruits of his creatures' transfers to the reborn community Jeremiah's designation of Israel as God's firstfruits, holy and set apart.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: God's creative word, 'Let there be light,' resonates with James's pairing of the Father of lights with the begetting 'word of truth' by which God gives new birth. Faint creation-by-word background.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: Wisdom present with God at creation provides a faint backdrop to God begetting believers by the word of truth as firstfruits of his creatures. Contested wisdom-cosmology resonance.

echoes.text: In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.
echoes.note: 'When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent.' James's counsel to be 'slow to speak' draws directly on the Wisdom tradition's repeated commendation of restrained speech.

echoes.text: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.' James's 'slow to anger,' with the claim that human anger does not produce God's righteousness, restates this Proverb's praise of restrained wrath.

echoes.text: Don’t be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.
echoes.note: 'Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools.' James's 'slow to anger' directly parallels Qoheleth's warning against hasty wrath.

echoes.text: Be swift to hear; And with patience make your answer. If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; And if not, let your hand be upon your mouth. Glory and dishonor is in talk: And the tongue of a man is his fall.
echoes.note: 'Be quick to hear, but deliberate in answering... let your life be sincere.' Sirach's near-identical counsel to be swift in listening and slow in reply is the closest extant verbal parallel to James's triad of swift-to-hear, slow-to-speak.

echoes.text: He who spares his words has knowledge. He who is even tempered is a man of understanding. Even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise. When he shuts his lips, he is thought to be discerning.
echoes.note: 'Whoever restrains his words has knowledge... even a fool who keeps silent is counted wise.' The pairing of measured speech with wisdom underlies James's swift-to-hear, slow-to-speak triad.

echoes.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
echoes.note: 'A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.' James's concern that the anger of man does not work God's righteousness resonates with the Proverbial linkage of speech and the management of anger.

echoes.text: Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
echoes.note: 'Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.' The warning against hasty speech reinforces James's slow-to-speak exhortation.

echoes.text: Unjust wrath can never be justified; For the sway of his wrath is his downfall. A man that is longsuffering will bear for a season, And afterward gladness will spring up to him; He will hide his words for a season, And the lips of many will tell forth his understanding.
echoes.note: 'Unjust anger cannot be justified... a wise man will hold his tongue until the right moment.' Sirach's linkage of controlled anger and restrained speech resonates with James's exhortation on listening, speaking, and wrath.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant law 'written on the heart' resonates faintly with James's 'implanted word which is able to save your souls,' an internalized word effecting salvation. Contested but thematically apt.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Moses insists the commandment is 'not too hard... but very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.' James's demand to be doers and not merely hearers of the word reflects the deuteronomic insistence that the word is given to be done.

echoes.text: They come to you as the people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain. Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them.
echoes.note: The people 'hear your words, but they will not do them'; the prophet is to them like a pleasant singer they enjoy yet disobey. James's hearers-who-are-not-doers, self-deluded, directly mirrors Ezekiel's indictment of those who listen without obeying.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s testimony is sure, making wise the simple.
echoes.note: 'The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul.' James's 'perfect law of freedom' that blesses the doer draws on the Psalter's praise of the perfect, soul-restoring Torah.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The doing of the law that culminates in love of neighbor (cited by James in 2:8) stands behind his 'perfect law of freedom' that demands enactment, not mere hearing. Faint anticipatory link.

echoes.text: Now, Israel, listen to the statutes and to the ordinances, which I teach you, to do them; that you may live, and go in and possess the land which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, gives you.
echoes.note: 'Listen to the statutes and rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live.' The hear-and-do-that-you-may-live formula resonates with James's promise that the doer of the work will be blessed.

echoes.text: All wisdom is the fear of the Lord; And in all wisdom is the doing of the law.
echoes.note: 'All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom there is the fulfilment of the law.' Sirach's pairing of wisdom with doing the law resonates faintly with James's doer-of-the-word who is blessed.

echoes.text: I said, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue. I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me.”
echoes.note: 'I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle.' James's image of bridling the tongue as the mark of true religion draws directly on the psalmist's resolve to muzzle his speech.

echoes.text: Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.
echoes.note: 'Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips.' The plea for divine restraint of the tongue parallels James's demand that the religious man bridle his tongue lest his religion be worthless.

echoes.text: Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Judge the fatherless. Plead for the widow.”
echoes.note: 'Bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause.' James's definition of pure religion as visiting orphans and widows in their affliction restates Isaiah's prophetic summons to care for the fatherless and the widow as the true worship God desires.

echoes.text: He does execute justice for the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, in giving him food and clothing.
echoes.note: God 'executes justice for the fatherless and the widow.' James grounds pure religion in imitating the God who defends orphans and widows, a defining mark of Israel's covenant ethics.

echoes.text: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
echoes.note: 'You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child.' The covenant law's protection of widows and orphans, with divine wrath against their oppressors, undergirds James's identification of their care as undefiled religion.

echoes.text: Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from troubles.
echoes.note: 'Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble.' The Wisdom commendation of tongue-control reinforces James's linkage of bridled speech with genuine piety.

echoes.text: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds; And till it come near, he will not be comforted; And he will not depart, till […]
echoes.note: 'He will not ignore the supplication of the orphan, nor the widow when she pours out her complaint.' Sirach's portrait of God hearing the cry of orphans and widows reinforces James's standard of true religion as their care.

echoes.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah! “What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?”, says Yahweh. “I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed animals. I don’t delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of male goats. When you come to appear before me, who has required this at your hand, to trample my courts? Bring no more vain offerings. Incense is an abomination […]
echoes.note: Isaiah rejects cultic observance divorced from justice, calling instead to 'wash yourselves... cease to do evil' and defend the oppressed. James's contrast of worthless versus pure-and-undefiled religion enacts this prophetic critique of empty ritual.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
echoes.note: 'Do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor.' Zechariah's prophetic restatement of covenant care for the vulnerable resonates with James's measure of authentic religion.

echoes.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
echoes.note: 'Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.' James's God-and-Father before whom pure religion attends to orphans and widows echoes this Psalmic title for the divine defender of the vulnerable.

echoes.text: Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no unclean thing! Go out of the midst of her! Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Touch no unclean thing... purify yourselves.' James's call to keep oneself 'unstained by the world' resonates faintly with the prophetic summons to ritual and moral purity over against defiling contact.

echoes.text: Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.
echoes.note: 'Be a father to orphans, and like a husband to their mother.' Sirach's exhortation to care for orphans and widows resonates with James's standard of pure religion, reinforcing the Wisdom tradition's mercy ethic.

echoes.text: “You shall also make a basin of brass, and its base of brass, in which to wash. You shall put it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it. Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in it. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they not die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh. So they shall wash their hands and their […]
echoes.note: The Pharisaic 'tradition of the elders' on washing hands before eating develops from priestly ablution law, where Aaron and his sons must wash hands and feet before approaching the altar. Mark frames the dispute against this Torah backdrop of ritual purity, though the hand-washing of laypeople before ordinary meals is an extension beyond the written commandment, which is precisely Jesus' point. Availability and thematic coherence are strong; verbal volume is faint.

echoes.text: On whatever any of them falls when they are dead, it shall be unclean; whether it is any vessel of wood, or clothing, or skin, or sack, whatever vessel it is, with which any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it will be clean. Every earthen vessel, into which any of them falls, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. All food which may be eaten, that on which water comes, shall be […]
echoes.note: The catalogue of washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and couches echoes Leviticus' rules on vessels rendered unclean by contact and requiring rinsing or breaking. Mark's parenthetical ethnography (7:3-4) presupposes this purity system as the matrix for the elders' tradition. The coherence is high though no single verse is quoted.

echoes.text: “‘Whoever he who has the discharge touches, without having rinsed his hands in water, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the evening. “‘The earthen vessel, which he who has the discharge touches, shall be broken; and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.
echoes.note: Leviticus 15 makes hands a vector of impurity (one with a discharge who has not rinsed his hands conveys uncleanness) and prescribes rinsing vessels of wood and breaking those of clay. This is among the few Torah texts tying hand-rinsing to purity, plausibly seeding the elders' extension to all meals. Faint and contested but availability is genuine.

echoes.text: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;
echoes.note: Formal citation introduced 'as it is written': 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' Mark follows the LXX, whose 'teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' supplies the polemical hinge against human tradition that the Hebrew lacks. Maximal volume, recurrence, and thematic coherence; this is the load-bearing OT text of the pericope.
echoes.lxxText: And the Lord has said, This people draw nigh to me with their mouth, and they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: Jesus cites the Decalogue commandment 'Honor your father and your mother' (attributed to Moses) as the divine command that Corban casuistry nullifies. Direct verbal quotation; the antithesis between this commandment and the tradition is the argument's spine.

echoes.text: “Anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
echoes.note: The paired citation 'He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death' quotes the capital statute of Exodus 21:17, reinforcing the gravity of the command being voided. Mark's wording tracks the LXX (kakologon). High volume and direct verbal correspondence.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic form of the honor-parents commandment is an equally valid source for 'Honor your father and your mother,' since Mark's citation could draw on either Decalogue. Listed as a parallel availability alongside Exodus 20:12; the verbal match is exact in both.

echoes.text: “‘For everyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death: he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood shall be upon him.
echoes.note: Leviticus 20:9 ('everyone who curses his father or mother shall be put to death') is a near-identical alternate source for the death-penalty clause and may stand behind Mark alongside Exodus 21:17. Strong availability; offered as parallel attestation.

echoes.text: When a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
echoes.note: The Corban dispute turns on the binding force of a vow dedicating property to God; Numbers 30 is the Torah's law of vows ('he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth'). Jesus' charge is that scribal handling of such irrevocable vows is used to override the prior duty to parents, so the vow legislation is the legal substrate of the controversy. Thematic coherence high; verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's vow law ('when you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay to pay it... that which has gone out of your lips you shall keep') reinforces the irrevocability that makes Corban exploitable. A secondary witness to the vow background behind 7:11-12.

echoes.text: “‘If it is an animal, of which men offer an offering to Yahweh, all that any man gives of such to Yahweh becomes holy. He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is changed shall be holy. If it is any unclean animal, of which they do not offer as an offering to Yahweh, then he shall set the animal before the priest; and the priest shall […]
echoes.note: Leviticus 27 governs things devoted/dedicated to the LORD (cherem and votive gifts), the legal category 'Corban, that is, given to God' invokes. Mark's transliterated technical term presupposes this dedication law; the abuse is treating a thing as devoted to bar a creditor-parent. Availability genuine, volume faint.

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: the life of the world to come

doctrine.title: General Rules
doctrine.article: doing good to bodies and souls

notes.text: The statutes — The laws which concern the worship and service of God. The judgments - The laws concerning your duties to men. So these two comprehend both tables, and the whole law of God.

In the sight of the nations — For though the generality of Heathens in the latter ages, did through inveterate prejudices condemn the laws of the Hebrew, yet it is certain, the wisest Heathens did highly approve of them, so that they made use of divers of them, and translated them into their own laws and constitutions; and Moses, the giver of these laws, hath been mentioned with great honour for his wisdom and learning by many of them. And particularly the old Heathen oracle expressly said, that the Chaldeans or Hebrew, who worshipped the uncreated God, were the only wise men.

So nigh — By glorious miracles, by the pledges of his special presence, by the operations of his grace, and particularly by his readiness to hear our prayers, and to give us those succors which we call upon him for.
So righteous — Whereby he implies that the true greatness of a nation doth not consist in pomp or power, or largeness of empire, as commonly men think, but in the righteousness of its laws.

glossa.text: *And now, O Israel, hear the precepts and the judgments. You shall not add.* He teaches the rule of equity, and strikes at every heresy. For he forbids to add anything of depraved intent to right doctrine, or to take away anything of the truth: for we must go by the royal way, not to the right hand or to the left; whence: *For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them ((Ose. XIV))*. In like manner John says: *If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book; if any man shall take away, God shall take away his part out of the book of life ((Apoc. XXII))*.

*Nor is there any other,* etc. There is not another nation so great, in dignity, namely, of gifts, not in the multitude of peoples. For neither did the nation of the Jews surpass other nations in number or in power, but by the prerogative of the fathers and by the divine favour.
*Which they have seen.* Sight holds the chief place among all the senses: therefore it is put for every sense.

notes.text: Who — Who shall so dwell in thy church here, as to dwell with thee forever in heaven?

Uprightly — Loving, and serving God, and loving his neighbour not in word only, but in truth; and this constantly. Worketh - Makes it his business to do justly, to give to every one his due, first to God, and then to men. Speaketh - His words and professions to God and men, agree with the thoughts and purposes of his heart.

He — He that doth not speak evil of his neighbour. neighbour - That is, any man. Nor taketh - Into his mouth, doth not raise it, neither spread or propagate it; or believe it without sufficient reason.

Vile — An ungodly man. honoureth - He highly esteems and loves them, though they be mean as to their worldly condition, and though they may differ from him in some opinions or practices of lesser moment. Sweareth - A promissory oath. Hurt - To his own damage. As if a man solemnly swear, that he will sell him such an estate at a price below the full worth; or that, he will give a poor man such a sum of money, which afterwards he finds inconvenient to him. Changeth not - His purpose, but continues firm and resolved to perform his promise.

To usury — In such a manner as is contrary to God's law: of which see otherwise, Exod. xxii, 25 Levit xxv, 36, 37, &c. Reward - Or, a bribe for him who hath a bad cause. Moved - He shall abide with God here, and when he dies be forever with the Lord. David professes his trust in God, his adherence to him and love of his people, ver. 1-3. His satisfaction in God, ver. 4-7. He speaks in the person of Christ, of Gods presence with him, of his resurrection and the glory that should follow, ver. 8-11. Michtam of David. Title of the psalm. Michtam - This seems to be a title belonging to the musick or the song, which, with the rest, is now lost and unknown. As David was both a member, and an eminent type, of Christ, he speaks of himself sometimes in the one and sometimes in the other capacity: and therefore having spoken of himself as a member of Christ, in the former part of the psalm, he proceeds to consider himself as a type of Christ, and being inspired by the holy Ghost: towards the close he speaks such things, as though they might be accommodated to himself in a very imperfect sense, yet could not properly, belong to any but to Christ, to whom therefore they are justly appropriated in the New Testament.

glossa.text: *He that. ((Ibid.))* The answer of the Lord, etc. *as far as* as Christ the lamb, without breaking of members, who properly entered the temple, not that he might be expiated like the rest, but without stain. *He worketh justice.* As when he cast out of the temple those that sold and bought.

*He that speaketh.* Here he follows it out more fully. Truth is when the thing is so as it is said: this Christ did properly. *In his heart,* who at times kept silence toward the unworthy who questioned him fraudulently. *He hath not wrought deceit.* Deceit is in the tongue, when one thing is said and another is in the breast. Or, *he hath not wrought deceit,* because all that he heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression, he made known to his neighbours, that is, to the disciples; to the Jews, his neighbours according to the flesh. *Nor hath he done evil to his neighbour.* But he prayed for them; he did not take up reproach against his neighbours, as is plain from this, that he did not tear Judas with a biting rebuke.

*To nothing,* etc. ((AUG.)) This is perfection, that the malignant one avail nothing in a man, and that this be in his sight, that is, that he know for certain that no one is malignant save he who turns from the Creator to created things. *The malignant one,* that is, the devil, is despised; as when he said: *Go back, Satan,* etc. On the contrary, *he glorifieth them that fear the Lord.* He swore, when he promised the apostles with most certain truth: *Now I will not call you servants, but friends.*

*He that sweareth to his neighbour,* etc. ((Ibid.)) These three things are not great, etc., *as far as* since in the conclusion above he set down a past tense, *he is brought to nothing.*

*Money.* Either it is earthly, which is utterly forbidden to be given out at usury, and which the Lord handed over to Judas to be paid out to the poor, not for usury. Or it is spiritual, which is commanded to be given out at usury, that is, preaching for the instructing of men. *And gifts against the innocent.* Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi, and daily devout offerings; but not against the innocent; rather he gave his soul for them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* Behold the complete answer to the questioner: he does them (he says), that he may invite us to the act, not only to the singing of them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* ((CASS.)) The conclusion. In like manner he that doeth these things shall rest on the mountain.

notes.text: No evil, but every good gift — Whatever tends to holiness. And every perfect gift - Whatever tends to glory. Descendeth from the Father of lights - The appellation of Father is here used with peculiar propriety. It follows, "he begat us." He is the Father of all light, material or spiritual, in the kingdom of grace and of glory. With whom is no variableness - No change in his understanding. Or shadow of turning - in his will. He infallibly discerns all good and evil; and invariably loves one, and hates the other. There is, in both the Greek words, a metaphor taken from the stars, particularly proper where the Father of lights is mentioned. Both are applicable to any celestial body, which has a daily vicissitude of day and night, and sometimes longer days, sometimes longer nights. In God is nothing of this kind. He is mere light. If there Is any such vicissitude, it is in ourselves, not in him.

Of his own will — Most loving, most free, most pure, just opposite to our evil desire, ver. 15. Begat he us - Who believe. By the word of truth - The true word, emphatically so termed; the gospel. That we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creatures - Christians are the chief and most excellent of his visible creatures; and sanctify the rest. Yet he says, A kind of - For Christ alone is absolutely the first-fruits.

Let every man be swift to hear — This is treated of from ver. 21 to the end of the next chapter. Slow to speak - Which is treated of in the third chapter. Slow to wrath - Neither murmuring at God, nor angry at his neighbour. This is treated of in the third, and throughout the fourth and fifth chapters.
The righteousness of God here includes all duties prescribed by him, and pleasing to him.

Therefore laying aside — As a dirty garment. All the filthiness and superfluity of wickedness - For however specious or necessary it may appear to worldly wisdom, all wickedness is both vile, hateful, contemptible, and really superfluous. Every reasonable end may be effectually answered without any kind or degree of it. Lay this, every known sin, aside, or all your hearing is vain. With meekness - Constant evenness and serenity of mind. Receive - Into your ears, your heart, your life. The word - Of the gospel. Ingrafted - In believers, by regeneration, ver. 18 and by habit, Heb. v, 14. Which is able to save your souls - The hope of salvation nourishes meekness.
Beholding his face in a glass — How exactly does the scripture glass show a man the face of his soul!
He beheld himself, and went away — To other business. And forgot - But such forgetting does not excuse.

But he that looketh diligently — Not with a transient glance, but bending down, fixing his eyes, and searching all to the bottom. Into the perfect law - Of love as established by faith. St. James here guards us against misunderstanding what St. Paul says concerning the "yoke and bondage of the law." He who keeps the law of love is free, John viii, 31, &c. He that does not, is not free, but a slave to sin, and a criminal before God, ver. 10. And continueth therein - Not like him who forgot it, and went away. This man - There is a peculiar force in the repetition of the word. Shall be happy - Not barely in hearing, but doing the will of God.

If any one be ever so religious — Exact in the outward offices of religion. And bridleth not his tongue - From backbiting, talebearing, evilspeaking, he only deceiveth his own heart, if he fancies he has any true religion at all.

The only true religion in the sight of God, is this, to visit — With counsel, comfort, and relief. The fatherless and widows - Those who need it most. In their affliction - In their most helpless and hopeless state. And to keep himself unspotted from the world - From the maxims, tempers, and customs of it. But this cannot be done, till we have given our hearts to God, and love our neighbour as ourselves.

glossa.text:
*Every gift,* etc. ((BED.)) After he had taught that vices are not to us from God, but from ourselves, etc., *as far as* the perfect gift can be understood.

*Nor of alteration.* No shadow shuts off his light, so as to send in any evils. Always the goods of light are in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes such as supervening sins overshadow.

*Of his own will.* Every good is from God, and you have not come to this by your own merits, but by the sole grace of the divine will. *That we might be some beginning,* etc. By this begetting let us not think that we are that which he himself is, but a certain primacy among creatures he granted to us by adoption. Whence another translator: *That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.*

*Slow to anger.* Let no one be angry rashly and without cause, whether against sinning subjects, or against any brethren whatsoever, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the ripeness of wisdom is not perceived save with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justice, yet cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, into which disturbance does not fall.

*Wherefore casting away,* etc. He has admonished them to seek out doctrine, for the receiving of which, and that they may be able to advance in it, he now exhorts to cleanness of body and of soul. For he who declines not from evil cannot do good. *The engrafted word.* That which by preaching we lay upon your hearts, or the word which was engrafted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you; now receive it more perfectly, and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery.

*To him that considereth the countenance.* He who purposes in his mind to consider in the Scriptures, as in a glass, the countenance of his nativity, how man is born, how frail, or what he shall be, of how brief an age, set in how many miseries, has contracted great compunction and a will of repenting; but straightway, seduced by some temptation, he forgets his compunction, and returns to sins. To this inconstancy he compares him who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between him who of his own accord, without a teacher, has applied himself to the Scriptures, and him who from another hears the Scriptures, since neither has fulfilled them.

When a boy is born he wails, whereby is signified the grief of the soul, and that it enters into life unto the miseries of the flesh, which grief the soul afterwards forgets, being accustomed to the enticements of the flesh.

*Not bridling his tongue,* etc. ((AUG., Serm. 3 ad fratres in eremo.)) What else is wordiness? etc., *as far as* and do thou diligently attend: *He that bridleth not his tongue, his religion is vain,* etc.

*And to keep himself unspotted from this world.* By *saeculum* he understands the world, or all the things which are in the world, as are the concupiscence of the flesh, and of the eyes, and the pride of life.

notes.text: Coming from Jerusalem — Probably on purpose to find occasion against him. Matt. xv, 1.
Washing of cups and pots and brazen vessels and couches — The Greek word (baptisms) means indifferently either washing or sprinkling. The cups, pots, and vessels were washed; the couches sprinkled.
The tradition of the elders — The rule delivered down from your forefathers.
Isaiah xxix, 13.

There is nothing entering into a man from without which can defile him — Though it is very true, a man may bring guilt, which is moral defilement, upon himself by eating what hurts his health, or by excess either in meat or drink yet even here the pollution arises from the wickedness of the heart, and is just proportionable to it. And this is all that our Lord asserts.

Wickedness — The word means ill natured, cruelty, inhumanity, and all malevolent affections. Foolishness - Directly contrary to sobriety of thought and discourse: all kind of wild imaginations and extravagant passions.

glossa.text: *And they come together. ((ID.))* It is plain how true is that confession of the Lord to the Father in which it is said: *Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones ((Matth. XI))*. The unlearned come, they bring the sick, that they may touch even his hem, and therefore, having desired health, they suffer. But the Pharisees and the Scribes, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, run together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but to the battles of questionings.

*With common hands. ((HIERON.))* By unclean, or common, hands he signifies the communion of the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the communion of the apostles does not wholly stretch out its branches as far as the sea. *Not washed.* They find fault over the unwashed hands of the body, though in their works nothing of uncleanness is found. They themselves, washed outwardly with water, are inwardly polluted with the rancour of conscience.

*The Pharisees. ((BEDA.))* The superstitious tradition of men, to wash the oftener, for the sake of eating and the like. But the necessary teaching of truth bids those who desire to eat the bread of life which came down from heaven to cleanse their works by the frequent lament of alms and of the other fruits of justice.

*Washings.* In vain do they keep the washings of vessels, who neglect the filth of their own hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, and the chastisement of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.

*Why do thy disciples,* etc. Wondrous folly! They accuse the Son of God because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works not of the body but of the soul, are to be washed, that the Word of God may be wrought in them.

*Well did he prophesy. ((HIERON.))* The fork of reason represses the barking of the Pharisees, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and of Isaias, that we too may be able to overcome heretics by the words of Scripture.

*There is nothing outside,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Nor is it the meat offered to idols, in so far as it is food, in so far as it is a creature of God, but the invocation of demons, that makes this unclean. Whence: *You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons ((I Cor. X))*.

The Jews boast themselves the portion of God, and call those foods common which all men use, such as oysters, hares, and animals of this kind, which do not divide the hoof, nor chew the cud, nor, among fishes, are scaly.

*From the heart of men. ((BEDA.))* The chief seat of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. They are also reproved, etc., *as far as* so that, if he has often seen us gaze upon a beautiful woman, he understands that we love her.
